summary.value: The paper introduces “Gaze on the Prize,” a plug-in framework for visual RL that learns a parametric foveal attention module—an anisotropic Gaussian with five parameters—applied to CNN feature maps to emphasize task-relevant regions (Section 3.2; Figure 1a). Attention is trained via return-guided contrastive learning: a buffer stores features and episode returns, k-NN mining (FAISS) forms triplets of similar states with higher/lower returns, and a triplet loss shapes attention to separate features predictive of success from failure, with spread regularization in log-space (Sections 3.3.1–3.3.2; Equations 1–5; Figure 1b–c). The approach integrates seamlessly with standard PPO and SAC without changing their core logic or hyperparameters, offering a lightweight, interpretable focus mechanism (Sections 3.1–3.2). Experiments on seven ManiSkill3 manipulation tasks, including cluttered variants, show consistent gains in sample efficiency and final performance; improvements reach up to 2.52× and enable solving tasks where baselines struggle (Section 5; Figure 2, Figure 4). Comparisons indicate structured foveal attention outperforms patch attention without contrastive learning (RQ1) and that return-guided supervision further boosts robustness under visual complexity (RQ2–RQ3; Figure 2). Ablations analyze buffer size and update frequency, and a compute study shows the added overhead is modest, dominated by triplet mining (Section 5.6; Table 1; Appendix B).

strengths.value:
1. Clear, focused novelty: learning a parametric “foveal” attention via return-guided triplet loss that explicitly separates “similar features with different returns” (Section 3.3.1; Equations 1–5; Figure 1b–c). This repurposes contrastive learning from encoder pretraining to directly shape spatial attention—distinct from CURL or RCRL (Section 2.2).

2. Minimal, interpretable attention design: a five-parameter anisotropic Gaussian head (“µx, µy, σx, σy, σxy”) that multiplies CNN feature maps (Section 3.2; Figure 1a). The log-space spread regularization (Equation 3) is a practical stabilization detail, and the single-fovea inductive bias is well justified for manipulation.

3. Strong plug-in story with careful engineering: attention learned on detached features stored in a persistent buffer, ensuring gradients update only the gaze head while “preserving the learned vision representations” and limiting compute/memory (Section 3.3.2). FAISS-based k-NN mining and clean positive/negative ordering by returns are spelled out concretely (k=16, top/bottom percentiles; Section 3.3.1–3.3.2; Table C1).

4. Broad and consistent empirical gains with actionable numbers: up to 2.52× sample-efficiency improvement and solving settings baselines fail (e.g., “only the contrastive variant reaches over 50%” on LiftPegUpright; “2.52×” on PokeCube; “1.86×” on PushT) (Section 5.2; Figure 2 center).

5. Robustness under clutter: return-guided attention markedly helps in “cluttered variants” (e.g., PushTClutter solved only with contrastive; PokeCubeClutter reaches 50% success with fewest steps) (Section 5.3; Figure 2 bottom), aligning with the paper’s thesis that task-aligned supervision filters distractors.

6. Cross-algorithm applicability: results transfer cleanly from PPO to SAC without altering “core logic or hyperparameters,” and outperform both CNN and CURL baselines in most tasks (Section 5.4–5.5; Figure 4). The direct CURL comparison with matched encoder and detailed implementation (Appendix C) strengthens fairness.

7. Causal ablations with concrete guidance: buffer-size study shows a sweet spot (100k) and highlights staleness effects at 200k; update-frequency study shows benefits of “every-iteration” contrast (Section 5.6; Figures 5–6). These yield practical tuning insights beyond headline results.

8. Compute transparency and practical relevance: a detailed overhead breakdown shows the gaze head is negligible (<0.05%) and that triplet mining (~12–13%) dominates, yet wall-clock to 50% success still improves (0.80× vs baseline) due to higher sample efficiency (Table 1; Appendix B Table B1).

9. Attention interpretability: qualitative maps demonstrate stable, localized focus vs. scattered patch attention (Figure 3), supporting the explainability claim with concrete visual evidence.

10. Well-structured experimental narrative: research questions (Section 4.1) organize results logically (Figure 2 top/center/bottom), with explicit task details and reward structure enabling return diversity (Appendix A.1–A.3), aiding reproducibility and clarity. Limitations are candidly scoped (sparse rewards; single fovea) (Section 6), increasing credibility.

weaknesses.value:
1. Novelty is incremental relative to return-based contrastive learning and parametric gaze models.
   - Evidence: Section 2.2 cites RCRL (Liu et al., 2021) that already uses returns to define contrastive objectives; Section 2.1 cites Gaussian/mixture parametric gaze and saliency models (Song et al., 2024; Reddy et al., 2020). Your contribution mainly couples a five-parameter Gaussian attention with return-guided triplets to shape spatial focus (Sections 3.2–3.3). Actionable: strengthen the novelty case empirically by (a) adding a “RCRL-style” baseline that applies return-based contrast at the encoder (not attention) with identical backbones, and (b) a “Gaussian attention + non-return contrastive” control (e.g., in-batch InfoNCE with strong augmentations) to isolate the return signal’s unique role. A positive result would more clearly separate your idea from known return-contrastive and gaze-parameterization lines.

2. Limited baseline coverage underrepresents strong visual RL alternatives.
   - Evidence: Only CURL is considered among contrastive baselines (Section 5.5; Figure 4), despite acknowledging augmentation-based successes and issues (Yarats et al., 2021). Patch attention is a weak spatial-attention baseline (1×1 conv; Section 5.1; Figure 2 top). Actionable: include DrQ/RAD-style data-augmentation baselines (Yarats et al., 2021) with matched backbones and hyperparameters; add a stronger spatial-attention baseline such as a spatial transformer or a small set of Gaussian kernels with learned mixing (vs. unconstrained patch attention). This will better position your approach among state-of-the-practice visual RL techniques.

3. Triplet supervision uses episode returns, which can be weakly localized and confounded.
   - Evidence: Triplets are built from neighbors in encoder space, separated by higher/lower episode returns (Section 3.3.1–3.3.2). Episode returns conflate many time steps and may differ for reasons unrelated to the current visual state (credit assignment), weakening the attentional signal. Actionable: evaluate alternatives that are more temporally local, e.g., using per-timestep advantage A_t, TD error, or n-step returns to label positives/negatives. Report a comparison on a subset of tasks (e.g., PushT, LiftPegUpright) to show which signal drives the most discriminative and stable attention.

4. Staleness and representation mismatch in the contrastive buffer are only partially addressed.
   - Evidence: Features are stored detached and later reweighted by current attention (Section 3.3.2), and larger buffers (200k) slow early learning due to “stale representations” (Figure 5). Actionable: (a) maintain a momentum/EMA encoder for the FAISS index to reduce mismatch; (b) periodically refresh a fraction of buffer embeddings; or (c) store raw observations and recompute features for mined triplets at mining time on a subsample to quantify the trade-off. A small-scale study on the PushT ablation setting would clarify whether the improved supervision justifies extra compute.

5. Single-fovea constraint likely limits multi-object attention; no empirical test of multi-fovea.
   - Evidence: The method predicts one Gaussian (Section 3.2) and acknowledges this limitation (Section 6). Tasks like PlaceSphere plausibly require simultaneous focus on gripper and receptacle (Figure 3 task context). Actionable: add a lightweight K=2–3 Gaussian mixture variant with a sparsity or entropy regularizer and evaluate where single-fovea underperforms (e.g., PlaceSphere, cluttered variants in Figure 2 bottom). This would turn a stated limitation into a concrete extension with measured benefits.

6. Statistical robustness and reporting are thin for the claimed gains.
   - Evidence: Results use three seeds with shaded standard error (Section 5), but there are no significance tests or aggregated tables beyond a few headline numbers (e.g., “2.52×,” “1.86×” in Section 5.2). Actionable: report per-task AUC or steps-to-X%-success with 95% CIs and significance tests across seeds for Figures 2 and 4; provide a summary table across all tasks. This will substantiate that improvements are consistent rather than due to variance.

7. Hyperparameter sensitivity is underexplored for the new components.
   - Evidence: Ablations cover buffer size and update frequency only (Section 5.6; Figures 5–6). Key design knobs (α in Eq. 1, λattn in Eq. 5, k in FAISS mining, top/bottom percentile thresholds, σtarget and λspread in Eq. 3) are fixed (Table C1). Actionable: add a one-task sweep (PushT) varying α, λattn, and k to demonstrate robustness; include at least one ablation on the percentile thresholds to ensure the “clean ordering” assumption is not brittle.

8. Attention “explainability” lacks quantitative evaluation.
   - Evidence: Figure 3 offers qualitative maps; no quantitative measure of whether attention covers task-relevant objects. Actionable: leverage simulator metadata in ManiSkill3 (Appendix A) to compute overlap (e.g., IoU) between attention heatmaps and known object masks or 2D projections of object bounding boxes, comparing foveal vs. patch attention and the effect of contrastive learning. This would substantiate the interpretability claim beyond visuals.

9. Generalization beyond fixed cameras and clutter is untested.
   - Evidence: Observations come from a fixed camera (Appendix A.2); robustness is only tested via clutter (Appendix A.4; Figure A1; Figure 2 bottom). Actionable: add evaluation under camera pose shifts or randomized intrinsics, and object texture/lighting randomization, to test whether return-guided attention transfers under modest viewpoint/appearance changes. This aligns with the stated goal of “robust” visual RL (Abstract; Section 1).

10. Overhead analysis is limited in scope and misses scaling behavior.
   - Evidence: Compute breakdown is reported for one setting (PushT; Appendix B; Table B1, Table 1), with triplet mining dominating (~12–13%). Actionable: (a) report memory overhead and FAISS index build/query times as buffer grows; (b) assess overhead under a larger encoder or higher image resolution (e.g., PPO’s 128×128 vs. SAC’s 64×64; Appendix D) to document scaling; (c) explore cheaper semi-hard in-batch mining as an alternative and report the performance/overhead trade-off.

11. Complementarity with augmentation-based contrastive is asserted but not demonstrated.
   - Evidence: Section 5.5 suggests the approaches are complementary and hints at “hybrid strategies,” but no experiment combines them. Actionable: include a small study adding random-crop InfoNCE (CURL-style) to your attention loss, or simply apply standard DrQ augmentations during RL updates alongside your attention objective, to validate the complementarity claim empirically.

12. PPO-only throughput/wall-time analysis obscures overall practical gains across tasks.
   - Evidence: Table 1 analyzes PushT only. Actionable: extend wall-clock and SPS reporting to at least two more tasks with different difficulty (e.g., LiftPegUpright, PokeCubeClutter) to show that “0.80× wall time to 50% SR” (Table 1) generalizes and to help practitioners reason about the compute/benefit trade-offs.

questions.value:
1. Clarify novelty vs. return-based contrastive RL
   - Section 2.2 cites RCRL (Liu et al., 2021), which already uses returns to define contrastive objectives. Please articulate the conceptual and algorithmic differences beyond moving the contrastive signal to a spatial attention head. A small, controlled baseline where the same return-guided triplet loss is applied to the encoder features (no attention) with identical backbones would isolate the unique benefit of shaping attention (Sections 3.3.1–3.3.2; Equations 1–5).

2. Gradient flow inconsistency
   - Early text says the auxiliary objective “affects both attention and policy/value learning” (lines 054–057), but Section 3.3.2 states stored features are “detached… preventing the contrastive loss from participating in vision backbone training.” Please clarify exactly which modules (encoder, attention, policy, critic) receive gradients from Lattn (Eq. 5) and how this interacts with LRL. A one-sentence summary and a small diagram extending Figure 1(a) would help.

3. Valid Gaussian parameterization and constraints
   - Section 3.2 predicts five parameters (µx, µy, σx, σy, σxy); Equation (3) regularizes σx, σy in log-space, but the paper does not state how σxy is constrained to ensure a positive semi-definite covariance. What parameterization do you use for σxy (e.g., ρ = tanh(·) with σxy = ρ σx σy)? Are µx, µy constrained to valid spatial ranges? Without these details, the attention could be invalid or unstable.

4. Choice of episode return as supervision
   - Triplets use episode returns (Sections 3.3.1–3.3.2). Because credit assignment can be diffuse, can you compare per-timestep advantage or TD-error labels versus episode returns on at least two tasks (e.g., PushT and LiftPegUpright)? This could strengthen the claim that “return differences reveal what matters” (lines 047–053).

5. Triplet mining specifics and sensitivity
   - Please detail: (a) how ties are handled when neighbors have equal returns; (b) how many anchors per iteration fail to find valid positives/negatives; (c) sensitivity to k = 16 and to the “top/bottom percentile = 50” choice (Table C1). A short sensitivity sweep would help validate the “clean ordering” assumption (Section 3.3.1).

6. Staleness in the contrastive buffer
   - Figure 5 suggests performance drops with a 200k buffer due to “stale representations” (Section 5.6). Could you evaluate one of: (a) an EMA/momentum encoder for the FAISS index; (b) periodic re-encoding of a small buffer fraction; or (c) re-encoding only mined triplets? Even a small-scale PushT study would clarify whether modest extra compute reduces staleness and improves early learning.

7. Stronger baselines
   - Beyond CURL (Figure 4), please add a DrQ/RAD-style augmentation baseline (Yarats et al., 2021) with matched backbones and hyperparameters, and a stronger spatial-attention baseline (e.g., spatial transformer or a small mixture of Gaussian kernels with learned mixing) to complement “patch attention” (Figure 2 top).

8. Multi-fovea extension
   - Section 6 notes the single-fovea limitation. Could you include a light K=2 mixture-of-Gaussians variant (with a sparsity or entropy regularizer) on one or two tasks where multiple regions plausibly matter (e.g., PlaceSphere; Figure 3 context)? Even preliminary results would substantiate the discussion.

9. Quantitative attention explainability
   - Figure 3 is qualitative. Given ManiSkill3 simulator metadata (Appendix A), can you report overlap between attention maps and 2D projections of task-relevant objects (e.g., IoU or center distance), comparing foveal vs. patch attention and the effect of contrastive learning (Figure 2 center/bottom)? This would directly support the interpretability claim.

10. Statistical robustness and summary metrics
   - Results are over three seeds (Section 5). Please report per-task steps-to-50% SR (and AUC) with 95% CIs and significance tests for Figures 2 and 4, and include a compact summary table across tasks. This would make the “up to 2.52×” and “1.86×” gains (Section 5.2) more compelling.

11. Generalization beyond fixed cameras
   - Observations come from a fixed camera (Appendix A.2). Could you test moderate camera pose/intrinsics perturbations or texture/lighting randomization to assess robustness and whether the learned fovea tracks task-relevant regions under viewpoint changes?

12. Sparse-reward stress test
   - Section 6 explains the limitation under sparse rewards. A small experiment that sparsifies rewards on one or two tasks (e.g., success-only bonus) would quantify failure modes and the extent to which contrastive supervision “collapses,” guiding future remedies (LLM-shaped rewards or curiosity).

13. Compute and memory scaling
   - Appendix B/Table B1 and Table 1 quantify compute on PushT. Please add: (a) memory footprint of the 100k FAISS buffer; (b) FAISS index build/query times vs. buffer size; (c) throughput for at least one additional task and for PPO’s 128×128 vs. SAC’s 64×64 encoders. Also report a cheaper in-batch semi-hard mining variant as a lower-overhead alternative, with performance trade-offs.

14. CURL fairness and complementarity
   - Appendix C applies augmentations only to CURL’s contrastive head. DrQ applies augmentations to RL updates. For fairness, could you compare against DrQ-style RL augmentations? Also, please test the suggested complementarity (Section 5.5) by adding a simple random-crop InfoNCE to your method or adding DrQ augmentations during RL alongside your attention loss on a subset of tasks.

15. Hyperparameter robustness
   - Beyond buffer size/frequency (Figures 5–6), please provide a small sweep on α (Eq. 1), λattn (Eq. 5), and k (Table C1), plus an ablation of the top/bottom percentile thresholds. This helps practitioners adopt your defaults with confidence.

16. Initialization and stability of the fovea
   - What are the initial values/ranges for µ and σ, and is there any warmup where Lattn (Eq. 5) is delayed until returns diversify? Did you observe early collapse to background or oscillatory attention without the log-space spread regularizer (Eq. 3)? A brief stability note would be useful.

17. Diagnostics on how attention helps learning
   - To better understand mechanisms, could you share auxiliary curves (e.g., critic loss, value error, policy entropy) comparing “foveal w/ vs. w/o contrastive” on PushT? This would indicate whether gains stem from improved value estimation, reduced gradient variance, or exploration effects.

18. Failure analysis where gains are marginal
   - For simple tasks where contrastive adds little (Figure 2 center; e.g., PushCube, PickCube), can you analyze whether attention converges to broad σ (near-uniform) or focuses on irrelevant regions? Short qualitative/quantitative notes would clarify when the method is most beneficial.

19. Triplet mining throughput vs. sample-efficiency trade-off across tasks
   - Table 1 shows PushT wall-time benefits despite overhead. Could you report wall-time to 50% SR for at least one more env (e.g., LiftPegUpright, PokeCubeClutter) to validate practicality beyond a single case?

20. Reproducibility clarifications
   - Section 4.2 mentions “lightly tuned” baselines. Please enumerate which hyperparameters deviated from ManiSkill3/CleanRL defaults per task to ensure fairness, and confirm that all random seeds and logging match the Reproducibility Statement (Section 8).
